name: Falcon 9 upper stage (2025-010D)
short_status: Hit the Moon on Aug 5, 2026 near Einstein crater: the spent second stage from the Falcon 9 that launched Blue Ghost 1 and Resilience in Jan 2025. Unintentional. LRO photographed the crater on Aug 11-12 and measured it at about 60 feet (18 m) across and under 10 feet (3 m) deep, centred at 19.4759 N, 266.7138 E.
tagline: SpaceX · United States · Rocket debris · 2026 · Commercial and multipolar Debris impact
stats: between finishing its mission and hitting the Moon

facts.label: What it was
facts.value: The Falcon 9 second stage from the 15 Jan 2025 launch of Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 1 and ispace's HAKUTO-R Mission 2 (Resilience), catalogued as COSPAR 2025-010D. Backward propagation of its orbit independently ties it to that launch.

facts.label: The launch
facts.value: 15 Jan 2025, 1:11 a.m. EST from Launch Complex 39A, Kennedy Space Center. Both landers were delivered successfully to their trans-lunar trajectories.

facts.label: Impact date
facts.value: 5 Aug 2026. The crater is now imaged and measured, but the impact TIME is still only predicted: Bill Gray gave 06:35:37.5 UTC and Campbell et al. 06:33:23 UTC plus or minus 55 seconds. Nothing observed the moment of impact, so no measured time exists.

facts.label: Where it hit
facts.value: 19.4759 N, 266.7138 E, at 511 m elevation, near the 181 km crater Einstein on the western limb. This is a measured position: the LRO team refined it by comparing images taken on 11-12 Aug 2026 against pre-impact ones. Earlier figures in circulation were predictions, and NASA reports the prediction proved accurate to about 0.6 miles.

facts.label: Near side or far side
facts.value: Genuinely unsettled. At roughly 93 to 94 degrees west the point sits essentially on the western limb. Gray places it on the near side; Campbell et al. and Korean coverage call it the far side; NASA says only "near the Einstein and Bell craters".

facts.label: Impact speed (predicted)
facts.value: 2.43 km/s, about 5,400 mph or 8,700 km/h. From the same orbital solution as the predicted position; no measured value has been published.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: Not measured. Published estimates run from about 4,000 kg (Fernando et al.) to about 4,900 kg (Gray). NASA's release gives no mass, despite the figure often being attributed to it.

facts.label: Why it hit the Moon
facts.value: Unintentional. SpaceX passivated the stage "per the appropriate rules and regulations", but stages sent on high-energy trajectories cannot be deorbited the way low-Earth-orbit stages can. NASA attributes the return to "solar activity and gravitational forces", and calls disposal on the lunar surface a technically accepted method rather than a violation.

facts.label: Was it a mission failure
facts.value: No. The stage had finished boosting both landers out of Earth orbit 19 months earlier. Blue Ghost 1 went on to land successfully and operate about 14 days; ispace's Resilience failed separately during its own descent in June 2025.

facts.label: Who tracked it
facts.value: Bill Gray of Project Pluto identified the collision course from 1,053 astrometric observations contributed by asteroid surveys and amateur astronomers at five observatories in Mississippi, Utah, Beijing and England. NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies at JPL later confirmed the impact was certain.

facts.label: Did anyone see it
facts.value: No spacecraft watched the impact itself. South Korea's Danuri orbiter imaged the site eight times, once about 30 minutes before and seven times afterwards, giving a rare before-and-after record from orbit, and its coordinates then helped LRO aim the imaging that measured the crater.

facts.label: What Danuri's images show
facts.value: A dark patch centred on the impact point with radial ejecta traces; the crater itself is not resolved. Danuri's terrain imager works at roughly 5 m per pixel, so a crater about 18 m across spans only a handful of pixels. KASA said on Aug 6 that the crater's size and shape were still being analysed; NASA published LRO's measurements on Aug 18.

facts.label: Crater size
facts.value: About 60 feet (18 m) across, measured where the rim stood out in the images, and less than 10 feet (3 m) deep, worked out from the length of its shadow. LRO's narrow-angle camera resolves features down to about 3 feet.

facts.label: What happens next
facts.value: Done: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter tilted to image the site on 11-12 Aug 2026 and published the results on Aug 18. Finding it took an unusual chain of hands: amateur astronomers spotted the trajectory, NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies refined it and passed the location to South Korea, Danuri photographed the site first and sent coordinates back, and LRO used those to aim its own follow-up.

facts.label: What Korea's space agency published
facts.value: KASA's own pre-impact plan gave a mass of about 4.9 tonnes, an impact speed of 2.43 km/s and a predicted crater 20 to 30 m across. Its post-impact release reports terrain change and ejecta traces near the site and states that the crater's size and shape are still being analysed. Neither release publishes coordinates.

facts.label: The policy question
facts.value: NASA and SpaceX say they are jointly studying how to prevent uncontrolled upper stage impacts on future high-energy missions in the Sun-Earth-Moon system.

timeline: Falcon 9 lifts off from Kennedy Space Center and delivers Firefly's Blue Ghost Mission 1 and ispace's Resilience to trans-lunar trajectories. The second stage, its job done, is left in a high Earth orbit.
Blue Ghost 1 lands successfully and operates about 14 days on the surface.
Resilience is lost during its own descent, a separate failure unrelated to the stage.
1,053 tracking observations have accumulated from asteroid surveys and amateur astronomers at five observatories, enough to show the abandoned stage is on a Moon-crossing path.
Jun to Aug 2026
Bill Gray revises the predicted impact repeatedly as new tracking arrives, once moving it about 170 km. NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies confirms the impact is certain.
Impact, near Einstein crater on the western limb. Nothing was in position to watch it happen.
5 to 6 Aug 2026
South Korea's Danuri images the site eight times, starting about 30 minutes before the impact.
KASA publishes the images, showing terrain change and ejecta traces, and says the crater's size and shape are still being analysed.
NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter tilts to photograph the site from several angles, catching the crater under different lighting.
NASA publishes the measured crater: about 60 feet across, under 10 feet deep, centred at 19.4759 N, 266.7138 E. The predictions were right to about 0.6 miles.
